newsitem.title: CUBA: FEATURE - Contrasts abound but Miami, Havana feed on one another.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Contrasts abound but Miami, Havana feed on one another.

text.p: The two cities lie separated by a narrow sleeve of water and a gaping ideological gulf, a study in opposites.

Yet Communist Havana and free-wheeling Miami are also bound inextricably together, joined by links of blood and money. From Havana to Miami the people flow, carrying the Spanish language and a Latin-Caribbean culture without which Miami would lose its unique flavor and pizzazz.

But most leave relatives behind. So from Miami to Havana the money flows, augmenting the threadbare budgets of hundreds of thousands of Cuban families and, some Miami-based emigres say, helping President Fidel Castro survive in power.
Tourist dollars are avidly sought in both cities, but the contrasts between them are stark and sometimes rich in irony.

Centuries-old colonial Havana crumbles in the tropical heat, its centre declared a protected World Heritage site by UNESCO. Parts are being refurbished by the government but many of its finest buildings lie derelict for lack of funds.
Few cars criss-cross its sleepy streets, and most are boxy Soviet-era Ladas, mingled with the occasional finned 1950s U.S. classic the size of a small boat.
Just across the Florida straits, supermodern Miami assails the visitor with soaring glass towers and sweeping expressways jammed with the latest-model sports cars.

Road skills appear lacking in both cities, though Havana is less dangerous in one regard: the drivers are far less likely to be armed. And visitors find Havana, unlike Miami, to be virtually free of violence.
A POLICEMAN EVERY 100 YARDS

"If something happens to you, the police don't just come looking for who did it but for who you were with, which is to say me," said Francisco, a worker at a state-run cafe in central Old Havana who declined to give his full name. "Look around, there is a policeman every 100 yards."

By contrast, a spate of shootings involving tourists lost in the seamier parts of Miami in recent years has obliged city authorities to put up road signs depicting a glowing orange sun along routes considered safe for visitors.

On chic Miami Beach, where restaurant staff appear to have stepped direct from the pages of Vogue, customers can spend a long time waiting for their existence to be acknowledged, let alone a menu or check, but the food will eventually arrive.
On a recent trip to a state-run Havana restaurant the attention was immediate but the resulting conversation proceeded as follows:
"Coffee, please."
"It will take an hour."
"What is there to eat for breakfast in the meantime?"
"Nothing."

In successive waves since the 1959 revolution, hundreds of thousands of Cubans have moved to Miami -- some 30,000 in the last big exodus in 1994 alone -- to build the approximately 800,000 strong Cuban community now living there.
MIAMI WITHOUT CUBANS = MINNESOTA

"Without the Cubans it would be like some kind of Minnesota here," said Julissa Mendoza, a 21-year-old Cuban-Honduran American, shouting over a pulsing salsa beat as she sold cigars at Mango's Tropical Cafe on Miami Beach. "That's what makes Miami as vivid as it is, the Cubans."
More than half of the two million people who live in and around Miami speak Spanish, and most of them are of Cuban origin. To those who remain in Cuba, they send back millions of dollars a year.

"The remittances signify for Cuba one of the main sources of income for the country," an economist at Havana's semi-independent Centre for Studies of the Cuban Economy told Reuters. "They could be the principal net inflow of foreign currency into Cuba."
He estimated the flow of funds sent by Cubans, almost all of them in Miami, at $500 million or more a year, about a sixth of Cuba's gross annual inflow of foreign funds.
"Most (Spanish-speaking) people in Miami are from the Havana region," a Western diplomat said, adding that the weighting of remittances towards Havana "has a distorting effect" on the Cuban economy.

Other diplomats in Cuba estimated the remittances at $400 million to $800 million a year. "That is a heck of a significant amount and probably is the underpinning of a lot of the economic activity," one said. "It does not take a lot to make the difference between surviving and not surviving here -- $20 in an envelope can do it."
ECONOMY NOT YET RECOVERED

Cuba's economy, although growing again, has not yet recovered from the severe contraction it underwent when Soviet economic support collapsed after the end of the Cold War. The average monthly salary of $10, even with two wage earners, covers only about half the basic food requirements of a family of four, the Cuban economist said.

After the recent introduction of direct telephone calls between Cuba and the United States -- mostly between Miami and Havana -- Cuba got $120 million as its share of receipts in 1995 alone, he said. "It must be around $200 millon now."

Ninoska Perez, spokeswoman for the Cuban American National Foundation in Miami, said her anti-Castro organisation did not object to remittances for humanitarian purposes but accused the Cuban government of taking a big slice for itself, diverting funds from the relatives it was intended for.
"A lot of people say that they won't send money as a matter of principle," she told Reuters. "Our first priority is to put an end to the problem in Cuba, and the problem is Castro."
